content: When you are pregnant, traveling to areas where malaria is prevalent significantly increases the risk of severe complications, including death, for both you and your unborn child. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advises continuing other malaria treatments, such as chloroquine, throughout pregnancy until delivery to protect the fetus from conditions like hemolytic anemia. After delivery, treatment with primaquine may be completed. It is currently unknown whether primaquine passes into breast milk. Before breastfeeding, your infant should be tested for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. Drug interactions can alter the effectiveness of your medications or increase the likelihood of serious side effects. It is essential to maintain a comprehensive list of all products you use, including prescription drugs, over-the-counter medications, and herbal supplements, and share this information with your healthcare provider and pharmacist. In the event of an overdose, if the individual exhibits severe symptoms such as loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately (911 in the U.S.). Otherwise, contact a poison control center right away. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222, and Canadian residents can call 1-844-764-7669. Laboratory and medical tests, such as G6PD blood tests and blood cell counts, should be conducted before starting this medication and periodically during treatment. Ensure you attend all scheduled medical and laboratory appointments. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is close to the time of your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular dosing schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. Store this medication at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. Primaquine is used in combination with other medications to prevent and treat malaria caused by mosquito bites in regions where malaria is common. Malaria parasites enter the body through mosquito bites and reside in tissues such as red blood cells or the liver. Primaquine is administered after other medications, like chloroquine, have eradicated the parasites in red blood cells. Primaquine then targets parasites in other tissues, preventing the recurrence of the infection. Both medications are necessary for a complete cure. The CDC provides updated guidelines and travel recommendations for malaria prevention and treatment worldwide. Take this medication orally as directed by your doctor, usually once daily. To minimize stomach upset, take it with food. Follow your doctor’s instructions precisely. Primaquine is typically taken for two weeks after leaving a malarious area. It is initiated during the last one to two weeks of other malaria treatments or immediately after completing them. The dosage depends on the type of infection and your response to treatment. Take this medication regularly and exactly as prescribed. Do not take more or less than directed, and do not stop taking it prematurely, even if you feel better, unless instructed by your doctor. Prevent mosquito bites by using insect repellents, wearing protective clothing, staying in air-conditioned or well-screened areas, using mosquito nets, and applying insect-killing sprays. Purchase insect repellents before traveling. The most effective repellents contain diethyltoluamide (DEET). No drug treatment is entirely effective in preventing malaria. Seek medical attention immediately if you develop symptoms of malaria, such as fever, chills, headache, or flu-like symptoms, especially while in a malarious area or even after completing this prescription. Common side effects of primaquine include nausea, vomiting, dizziness, stomach upset, and abdominal cramps. Remember that this medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Serious allergic reactions to this drug are rare. This is not a complete list of possible side effects. In the U.S., contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. In Canada, consult your doctor for medical advice about side effects. Before taking primaquine, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it or have any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that can cause allergic reactions or other issues. This drug may cause dizziness. Alcohol or marijuana (cannabis) can exacerbate dizziness. Avoid driving, operating machinery, or performing tasks requiring alertness until you can do so safely. Limit alcoholic beverages. Primaquine may cause a condition affecting heart rhythm (QT prolongation). The risk of QT prolongation may increase if you have certain medical conditions or are taking other drugs that can cause QT prolongation. Low levels of potassium or magnesium in the blood may also increase your risk of QT prolongation. This risk may be heightened if you use certain drugs (such as diuretics or water pills) or have conditions like severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting. This medication must not be used during pregnancy as it may harm an unborn baby. Women of childbearing age should undergo a pregnancy test before starting this medication. It is crucial to prevent pregnancy during and after treatment with primaquine. Both men and women must use reliable forms of birth control, such as condoms or birth control pills, during treatment. Men should continue using birth control for at least three months after completing treatment, and women should continue for at least one menstrual cycle after treatment ends. If you become pregnant or suspect you may be pregnant, inform your doctor immediately. While pregnant, traveling to a malaria-endemic area poses a significantly higher risk of death and other complications for both you and your infant. The CDC recommends continuing other malaria treatments, such as chloroquine, throughout pregnancy until delivery to prevent harm to the unborn baby, such as hemolytic anemia. After delivery, you may complete treatment with primaquine. It is unknown whether this drug passes into breast milk. Your doctor should test your infant for G6PD deficiency before breastfeeding.
